system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
The patient was diagnosed with sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis (lung infection caused by the TB bacteria) in 2019. He was admitted to the hospital on 03/02/2020 and discharged on 09/05/2020, staying for 3 months, 6 days, and 7 hours in a ward bed. The insurance payer was listed as sus. He was referred to the hospital because he had a persistent dry cough for 4 weeks, without coughing up any phlegm, along with night sweats. Three days before admission, he had a fever (which was not measured) and difficulty breathing. One day before admission, he had sudden pain in the right side of his chest that spread to the right side of his neck, and his breathing difficulty got much worse. He did not cough up any blood. He mentioned that he had been in prison for about 3 years out of the last 6 years and had no symptoms since then. He also reported losing about 8 kg in weight one month ago. He did not have any changes in his urine or bowel movements.

On examination, he looked generally well but was pale (pale skin), hydrated, and not blue in color. He was conscious and aware of his surroundings. His heart sounds were normal, with a heart rate of 85 beats per minute (normal range is 60 to 100 beats per minute, so his was within the normal range). When listening to his lungs, normal breath sounds were heard on the left side, but no sounds were heard on the right side, and the right side of his chest did not expand as much as the left. His oxygen saturation was 98% (normal is 95% or higher, so this was within the normal range). His abdomen was flat and soft, with normal bowel sounds and no signs of infection in the abdominal lining. His legs had no swelling and no signs of blood clots. His surgical wound was dry and in good condition, with stitches intact.

Tests were done to confirm the type of TB. A sputum (phlegm) sample collected on 02/03/2020 was tested using a DNA method called Geno Type MTBDR Plus. The result showed the TB bacteria were sensitive to rifampin and isoniazid, meaning these medicines would work against his infection. Another sputum sample collected on 02/03/2020 was tested using a microscope method called Ziehl-Neelsen. The result was positive, showing 10 to 99 bacteria in 100 fields of view, which confirms the presence of TB.

During his stay, he had several complications related to the TB. First, he had a spontaneous pneumothorax (air leaking into the space around the lung, causing it to collapse) on the right side. A chest drain (a tube placed in the chest to remove air or fluid) was put in on 03/02/2020. A pleurostomy (a procedure to create an opening in the chest wall to drain fluid) was done on 03/03/2020. The pleurostomy was closed, but the lung collapsed again, so a pleural drain and a Heimlich valve (a one-way valve attached to the drain to let air out but not back in) were used on 10/03. The Heimlich valve was removed on 27/03, but the drain was kept open. A new pleurotomy (another chest opening) was done on 31/03. On 07/04, he had an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (a major surgery to open the chest to look inside) because of bleeding from TB cavities (hollow spaces in the lung caused by TB). There was significant oozing bleeding. The cavity was packed with compresses (gauze pads) to stop the bleeding. On 11/04/2020, he had a right pneumonectomy (surgical removal of the entire right lung) through a lateral thoracotomy (side chest incision). A tracheostomy (a small opening made in the windpipe to help with breathing) was also done. This surgery went without complications. The chest drain and tracheostomy tube were removed on 06/06.

He also had surgical wound infections caused by a type of bacteria called Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (a germ that is hard to kill with common antibiotics). He was treated with three antibiotics: Vancomycin (an antibiotic to fight the infection), Meropenem (another strong antibiotic), and Amikacin (an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection). The antibiotic treatment was stopped on 02/04 after he improved clinically and his procalcitonin level (a blood test that shows how severe a bacterial infection is) was 0.09 (a low level, indicating the infection was under control).

On 07/04, he had hypovolemic shock (a dangerous drop in blood pressure due to losing too much blood) because of bleeding from the surgical wound and the pleurostomy site. This required urgent surgery. On 10/04, he had a cardiopulmonary arrest (his heart and breathing stopped) for 4 minutes due to asystole (a flatline where the heart does not beat) caused by low oxygen levels (hypoxia). He was resuscitated and recovered.

At discharge, he was in good general condition with no complaints. He was continuing his TB treatment with RI (Rifampin and Isoniazid). He was given 2 months of prescriptions. He was also continuing oral iron replacement (medicine to treat low iron levels). A meeting was held with [person], along with the thoracic surgery team, to explain the condition and treatment. [person] understood the instructions and appreciated the care. Exams were requested for a follow-up appointment. A follow-up was scheduled at [organization] and with the thoracic surgery team. [person] was advised about warning signs and told to call if he had any concerns. A report was provided, and [organization] was contacted for assisted treatment involving infectious diseases and thoracic surgery.
